title: JPA and Hibernate: mapping, loading strategies and optimistic locking
description: JPA mappings, lazy versus eager loading, open-in-view, N+1 and its fixes in Spring Data JPA, paging with collection fetches, insert batching and @Version locking.
source: Hibernate ORM user guide (fetching, batching, locking); Spring Data JPA documentation (Page, EntityGraph, projections); Spring Boot reference (spring.jpa.open-in-view); Vlad Mihalcea on Hibernate performance; Baeldung
seriesDescription: ORM, lazy loading and N+1, transactions, JdbcTemplate, HikariCP and migrations. JEE-Advanced style: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code and multi-correct questions.

questions.prompt: Match each JPA/Hibernate attribute to what it does.

right.text: Marks the inverse side; the other side owns the foreign key
Names the foreign-key column on the owning side
Propagates persist, merge and remove from parent to children
Deletes a child row once it is removed from the parent's collection
Adds a counter that is checked in the `UPDATE`'s `WHERE` clause
Forces the association to load eagerly
Generates the primary key from a sequence

questions.explanation: The owning side (the one without `mappedBy`, usually the `@ManyToOne`) is the only side Hibernate uses to write the foreign key. `cascade` moves operations down the tree, `orphanRemoval` deletes de-referenced children, `@Version` enables optimistic locking.

questions.prompt: Complete the JPA fundamentals by dragging the right words into the blanks.
questions.text: A JPA entity needs a no-argument constructor and an {1} field. In a bidirectional association the side that declares {2} is the inverse side and does not write the foreign key. Store enums with @Enumerated({3}) so reordering the constants cannot corrupt data. Changing a managed entity inside a transaction is persisted by {4} at flush time, without calling save().
questions.explanation: `ORDINAL` stores the position of the constant, so inserting a new constant in the middle silently remaps old rows. Dirty checking compares each managed entity with its loaded snapshot at flush and issues `UPDATEs` for the differences.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the option that fits.
questions.assertion: With Spring Boot's default `spring.jpa.open-in-view=true`, a controller can still read a lazy collection of an entity returned by a service method.
questions.reason: The `EntityManager` stays bound to the web request thread until the response is rendered, so the Hibernate `Session` is still open.

whys.a: True: the Session is still open, so the lazy proxy can initialise.
whys.b: R is the mechanism itself, so this option wrongly says it does not explain A.
whys.c: R is true here, so this option wrongly says it is false.
whys.d: A is true, so this option wrongly says it is false.

questions.explanation: Open `Session` In View keeps the persistence context open for the whole request. It hides `LazyInitializationException` but holds a database connection until rendering ends and encourages N+1 in the view layer; many teams set it to false.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the option that fits.
questions.assertion: A `@ManyToOne` association is `EAGER` by default in JPA, so loading an `OrderLine` also loads its `Order`.
questions.reason: `FetchType.EAGER` guarantees that one SQL `JOIN` is used in every query that loads the entity.

whys.a: R is false, so it cannot be the explanation of A.
whys.b: R is false, so this option wrongly calls both statements true.
whys.c: Correct: A is true (ToOne defaults to EAGER) but R is false; EAGER only says the data must be loaded, not how.
whys.d: A is true, so this option wrongly says it is false.

questions.explanation: `EAGER` with `em.find()` usually becomes a `JOIN`, but with `JPQL`, Criteria or Spring Data queries Hibernate runs the query first and then fires secondary `SELECTs` per row, which is a classic hidden N+1. Prefer `LAZY` everywhere and fetch explicitly per use case.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the option that fits.
questions.assertion: A JPQL bulk statement such as `"UPDATE Product p SET p.price = 0"` automatically increments the `@Version` column of the rows it touches.
questions.reason: For managed entities, the `UPDATE` that Hibernate flushes carries `WHERE id = ? AND version = ?`.

whys.a: A is false, so this option wrongly accepts both.
whys.b: A is false, so this option wrongly says both are true.
whys.c: R is true, so this option wrongly says it is false.
whys.d: Correct: bulk statements bypass the persistence context and do not touch the version (HQL needs "update versioned" to do that); R describes the managed-entity path correctly.

questions.explanation: Bulk `JPQL/HQL` and native SQL updates skip dirty checking, the first-level cache and version checks, so the version column is not touched by default. Hibernate's HQL has an opt-in keyword (`update versioned Product ...`), or you can bump the column yourself (`set p.version = p.version + 1`); otherwise avoid mixing bulk updates with versioned entities.

questions.prompt: 50 `Author` entities are loaded with one query. `Author.books` is `LAZY` and mapped with `@BatchSize(size = 10)`. A loop then calls `author.getBooks().size()` for every author. Counting the first query, how many `SELECT` statements does Hibernate run?
questions.explanation: The first touch of an uninitialised collection loads the collections of up to 10 not-yet-loaded owners with one `IN` query, so 50 authors need 5 batches: `1 + 5 = 6`. Without `@BatchSize` it would be `1 + 50 = 51`.

questions.prompt: Select all valid ways to avoid the N+1 select problem when listing authors together with their books in Spring Data JPA.

options.text: A `@Query` with `JOIN FETCH` on the books association.
options.why: Right: one SQL statement returns authors and books together.

options.text: `@EntityGraph(attributePaths = "books")` on the repository method.
options.why: Right: it adds the fetch join declaratively.

options.text: A DTO or interface projection that selects only the needed columns in one query.
options.why: Right: no entities, no lazy loading, no N+1.

options.text: Marking `Author.books` as `FetchType.EAGER` globally.
options.why: JPQL and derived queries still load the collection with extra selects per author.

options.text: Setting `spring.jpa.show-sql=true`.
options.why: It only logs the statements; it does not change them.

questions.explanation: Fix N+1 per use case (fetch join, entity graph, projection, batch fetching) instead of changing the mapping to `EAGER`. Detect it by logging statements or asserting query counts in tests.

questions.prompt: `GET /authors?page=0&size=20` must return authors with their books. A `JOIN FETCH` on the books collection combined with `Pageable` makes Hibernate log that it applies `firstResult/maxResults` in memory. What is the usual fix?

options.text: Page the authors alone, then batch-load their books with `@BatchSize` or a second `IN` query.
options.why: Right: the limit applies to authors in SQL and the children arrive in one extra statement.

options.text: Switch `Author.books` to `FetchType.EAGER` so the join happens automatically.
options.why: `EAGER` does not change how a paged JPQL query works and can add secondary selects.

options.text: Keep the `JOIN FETCH` and raise the page size so that the in-memory paging stays cheap enough.
options.why: Hibernate would load every author and book row into memory and page there.

options.text: Turn on open-in-view so the books are fetched lazily while serialising.
options.why: That is exactly N+1: one select per author while rendering JSON.

questions.explanation: A join to a collection multiplies parent rows, so SQL `LIMIT` would cut rows, not authors; Hibernate therefore pages in memory and logs a warning (`HHH000104` in Hibernate 5, `HHH90003004` in Hibernate 6). Split into two steps: page the parents first, then load the children with an `IN` query or `@BatchSize`. Setting `hibernate.query.fail_on_pagination_over_collection_fetch=true` turns the silent fallback into an error.

questions.prompt: Entity `Author` has a `List<Book> books`. In the Spring Data JPA interface `AuthorRepository`, declare a method `findAllWithBooks()` that returns `List<Author>` and loads every author together with its books in the same `SELECT`.

checks.label: fetches books in the same query (JOIN FETCH or an entity graph)

questions.model:
@Query("select distinct a from Author a join fetch a.books")
List<Author> findAllWithBooks();
questions.explanation: `DISTINCT` removes duplicate `Author` references produced by the join (Hibernate 6 de-duplicates automatically). An `@EntityGraph` on an overridden `findAll()` is an equally valid solution.
questions.starter:
public interface AuthorRepository extends JpaRepository<Author, Long> {
    
}

questions.prompt: Add optimistic locking to the JPA entity `Product`: write the version attribute (the annotation and the field) that Hibernate checks and increments on every update.

checks.label: declares a numeric or timestamp field

questions.explanation: Hibernate adds `"AND version = ?"` to the `UPDATE` and increments the value; if zero rows match it throws `OptimisticLockException` (wrapped by Spring as `ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException`). Prefer a numeric counter over a timestamp.

questions.prompt: Two users edit the same `Product` form. The second save fails with `ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException`. What should a REST API normally do?

options.text: Return `409 Conflict` (or 412 with `ETag`) and let the client reload and re-apply its change.
options.why: Right: the data changed underneath the client, so the user or client must merge.

options.text: Retry the identical `UPDATE` in a loop until it finally succeeds, as the conflict is only transient.
options.why: The stale version never matches again, so the loop would fail or need a reload anyway.

options.text: Return 500 and alert, because it is an unexpected server error.
options.why: It is an expected concurrency outcome and should map to a client-level conflict.

options.text: Remove `@Version` so later saves silently overwrite the first one.
options.why: That brings back lost updates.

questions.explanation: Optimistic locking detects, it does not resolve, a conflict. Automatic retry is only safe for server-side read-modify-write that re-reads the row in each attempt.

questions.prompt: An `import` job calls `repository.saveAll(...)` with 5,000 new entities and `hibernate.jdbc.batch_size=50`, yet the SQL log shows 5,000 separate `INSERT` statements on PostgreSQL. Which cause is the most likely?

options.text: The id is mapped with `GenerationType.IDENTITY`, so Hibernate must run each `INSERT` at once to learn the key.
options.why: Correct: the generated key is needed when `persist()` returns, so inserts cannot be queued and grouped at flush time.

options.text: `hibernate.jdbc.batch_size` only applies to `UPDATE` statements, never to `INSERTs`.
options.why: Batching works for `INSERT`, `UPDATE` and DELETE when the id strategy allows it.

options.text: `saveAll` always issues one statement per entity because it runs inside a transaction.
options.why: Transactions do not prevent batching; batching is applied to the statements inside a transaction.

options.text: `spring.jpa.open-in-view` is true, and that setting disables JDBC batching for inserts.
options.why: Open-in-view only keeps the session open during rendering and has no effect on statement batching.

questions.explanation: `IDENTITY` disables insert batching in Hibernate. Use a `SEQUENCE` generator (with an `allocationSize` that matches the database sequence increment) and consider `hibernate.order_inserts=true`; on MySQL, which has no sequences, accept the cost or batch with plain JDBC.

questions.prompt: Entity `Order` declares `@OneToMany List<Line> lines` with neither `mappedBy` nor `@JoinColumn`, and `Line` has no field pointing back to `Order`. When Hibernate generates the schema, how many tables does it create for these two entities in total, counting any link table?
questions.explanation: A unidirectional `@OneToMany` without `@JoinColumn` is mapped through a join table (`orders_lines`), so the tables are `orders`, `line` and the link table: 3. Add `@JoinColumn(name = "order_id")` or make it bidirectional with `mappedBy` to keep the foreign key in the `line` table and drop the extra table.

questions.prompt: True or false: inside a `@Transactional` method, changing a field of an entity that was just loaded through the repository is written to the database at commit even if `save()` is never called.

options.text: True
options.why: Correct: the entity is managed, so dirty checking at flush time issues the UPDATE.

options.text: False
options.why: Wrong: the persistence context compares managed entities with their loaded snapshot and writes the difference.

questions.explanation: Calling `save()` on a managed entity is redundant but harmless. It matters for new entities and for detached ones, which need `merge` semantics.

questions.prompt: True or false: Hibernate's first-level cache (the persistence context) is shared by all threads and requests of the application.

options.text: True
options.why: Wrong: it is bound to one `EntityManager` and so to one unit of work.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: each `EntityManager` has its own persistence context; sharing across requests would need the second-level cache.

questions.explanation: The first-level cache gives repeatable reads of entities inside one transaction and one thread. The optional second-level cache is the shared, `SessionFactory`-wide one.
